health_findings.claim: The window suite has two rules for timing assertions on a shared machine. M-001 is kept out of `-Case All` because 'Timing on a shared machine: these are measurements'. T-005 asserts UI-thread latency (every phase's max under 1 s, p95 under 200 ms) and is in All. SL-044's own record shows T-005's longest wait reaching 857 ms against the 1 s bar, depending on the display state. A busy machine can therefore fail -Case All with no defect in the code.
health_findings.evidence:
WindowCases.ps1:2637: All includes 'T-005'. WindowCases.ps1:2574-2577 asserts max < 1000 and, with enough probes, p95 < 200. WindowCases.ps1:32-34 and SL-039-live-results.md:157-158 exclude M-001 from All for timing on a shared machine. SL-044-folder-tree.md:162-171 reports longest waits of 378 to 857 ms in one batch and says two batches of the same runs 'came out two ways'.
Fix: Treat T-005 like M-001: run it only when named, and report its numbers. Or keep in All only its non-timing checks (the window moved, five phases sampled), and move the latency bars to a case that runs only when named.

health_findings.claim: SmbRig.cs is compiled into two projects, and each pins its own SMBLibrary versions. Only a comment says 'The same versions as tests/FsAnalyser.Core.Tests'. The rig calls a private overload of SMBServer.Start by reflection with an exact parameter list, so bumping the package in only one project compiles cleanly and then fails at run time in that one, with 'SMBLibrary no longer has SMBServer.Start(...)'. The failure lands in the opt-in network cases that run least often.
health_findings.evidence:
StallRig.csproj:17 links SmbRig.cs, and StallRig.csproj:21-23 pins SMBLibrary 1.5.8.1 and SMBLibrary.Win32 1.5.8. FsAnalyser.Core.Tests.csproj:19-20 pins the same two separately. SmbRig.cs:68-71 does the reflection with a fixed parameter-type list.
Fix: Pin the two versions once: a Directory.Packages.props with central package management, or a shared MSBuild property in Directory.Build.props that both csproj files use.
(seen by structure)

health_findings.claim: The window cases take a file's size on disk to equal its size ('on any NTFS volume with clusters of 64 KiB or less, without asking the volume'). That fails when %TEMP% is inside an NTFS-compressed folder, e.g. a drive set to 'Compress this drive to save disk space'. New-File writes all-zero bytes, and a compressed 64 KiB zero file takes 0 bytes on disk. Every on-disk check then fails as if the app had miscounted: OutcomeDetail's 'taking X on disk', largestFileOnDisk, and the tree's on-disk figures, order and shares. The failure never names the cause. TempTree checks for NTFS (TempTree.cs:26-28) but not for the Compressed attribute, and its TextFile compresses without Compress(). There the counting-rule tests' on-disk and probe counts shift in the same unexplained way.
health_findings.evidence:
I reproduced it in .health-scratch/compressed-temp. After 'compact /c' on the folder, [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes(zeros.bin, [byte[]]::new(64KB)), as New-File does, gave attributes Archive, Compressed. After the flush, compact reported '65536 : 0 ... zeros.bin' and GetCompressedFileSizeW returned 0 for it. A 64 KiB Random(20) file (TempTree's pattern) returned 65536. The header claim is at WindowCases.ps1:16-18, and New-File is at :169-172 ([byte[]]::new($bytes)).
Fix: In New-CaseFolder (and the TempTree constructor), refuse with a named reason when the new folder has FileAttributes.Compressed, the way TempTree refuses a volume that is not NTFS. Alternatively, clear the attribute on the fresh folder with 'compact /u'. Also have New-File write incompressible bytes, as TempTree.Pattern does.
(seen by find:3:1; reproduced)

health_findings.claim: Two pieces of hook code run on the app's UI thread with no try/catch. One is WatchList's Background-priority callback, which reads LastRefresh. The other is Measure's ScanningPanel visibility handler, which reads SkippedRefreshes while the app collapses ScanningPanel in StartScan's finally. WindowState throws when a property is missing or of another type. In the first, the throw reaches Dispatcher.UnhandledException, because BeginInvoke(priority, lambda) uses the legacy delegate semantics. In the second, it escapes the app's own async void StartScan. Either way report mode ends with Discard and exit 70, no report and no 'refused' line. So after an app-side rename of one of these internal properties, L-001, L-002, M-001 and the watch runs of B-007/B-008 fail as an app crash rather than a hook refusal. The hook's own rule at AfterList says 'Never onto the dispatcher: the app would take it for its own fault and exit 70.'
health_findings.evidence:
StartupHook.cs:669-673 is app.Dispatcher.BeginInvoke(DispatcherPriority.Background, () => { seen.RefreshMs.Add(WindowState<TimeSpan>(window, "LastRefresh")...); ... }). StartupHook.cs:783-794 is AddValueChanged(panel, ...) calling WindowState<int>(window, "SkippedRefreshes") inside the Log argument. WindowState at :831-833 throws InvalidOperationException. The comment at :543 is 'Never onto the dispatcher: the app would take it for its own fault and exit 70.' Act's comment at :921 confirms that BeginInvoke exceptions reach the app's handler. App.xaml.cs:84-89 is DispatcherUnhandledException leading to Discard and Shutdown(70). MainWindow.xaml.cs:237 sets ScanningPanel.Visibility = Collapsed inside the finally.
Fix: Wrap both callbacks' bodies in try/catch that logs 'refused mode=... reason=...', as AfterList and StartSecondScan do.
(seen by find:3:1)
